title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
The failure here is a model asserting fabricated information as fact: an AI tool produced nonexistent case citations, invented case titles, and false legal holdings, all of which were then submitted to a court in multiple filings. The tool, named Irys, was used by a lawyer who believed it was connected to a verified legal research subscription and would check its own citations. That belief was mistaken, and no independent verification step was performed before the filings were submitted. The fabrications were caught not by the submitting lawyers but by opposing counsel.

The deployment failure occurred at the point of human reliance. A lawyer applied an AI tool outside the conditions she understood it to operate under, and no review process caught the errors before they entered the court record. Catching this would have required a lawyer to look up each cited case in a primary legal database before filing, a step the submitting attorney assumed the tool had already performed.

What is not established is whether State Farm directed or knew about the use of the AI tool, or whether any court sanction has yet been issued as a result of the admitted hallucinations.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers in a Los Angeles lawsuit have admitted to using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases and citations in their court filings. The homeowner's attorney discovered that the motions contained nonexistent cases, fabricated quotes, and false legal holdings. The lawsuit involves Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, whose Carson home was damaged by fire in 2020, and later suffered water damage during repairs. After State Farm allegedly delayed approving repairs, the reconstruction was never completed, leaving Meni-Siliga and her husband bankrupt and homeless after draining their savings and retirement accounts. State Farm named them, the contractor, and a public adjuster as defendants in their original answer to the complaint.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted she used an AI tool called Irys to help prepare filings, mistakenly believing it was connected to her law firm's Westlaw subscription and would verify citations. She confirmed that seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and fake quotes. Lead counsel Kenneth Katel apologized to the court and accepted responsibility for the filings. The trial is scheduled for October. AI hallucinations in legal work are becoming increasingly common, with 41 percent of law firms now using generative AI, and a database tracking 1,922 documented cases of legal hallucinations worldwide.
